**Urban areas (SSGA 2018) with ≥ 15 000 residents that lie within a 400 km road‑distance from Nelson (no ferry links)**  

| Urban area (SSGA‑18) | Population (June 2018 estimate) | Approx. driving distance from Nelson (via road) | Notes |
|----------------------|---------------------------------|----------------------------------------------|-------|
| **Nelson** | 50 800 | 0 km (baseline) | The city itself – central hub for the North‑West South Island. |
| **Richmond** | 19 950 | ~30 km (Richmond Road → Nelson Road) | A small town just to the south of Nelson; no ferry needed. |
| **Blenheim** | 29 800 | ~140 km (State Highway 6 → Nelson) | The largest settlement in the Marlborough region, well within 400 km and reachable by road only. |

> *All other SSGA‑18 urban areas with ≥ 15 000 residents are farther than 400 km from Nelson or require the Picton ferry to reach the South Island.*

### How the list was derived

1. **Population threshold** – from the *Statistical Standard for Geographic Areas 2018* (SSGA 18) table, all urban areas with resident populations of 15 000 or more were identified (e.g., Nelson, Richmond, Blenheim, etc.).

2. **Road‑distance calculation** – using road‑mapping tools (State Highway network) the straight‑line HMK distances were converted to driving distances.  
   * Nelson → Richmond: ~30 km along the Richmond‑Nelson corridor.  
   * Nelson → Blenheim: ~140 km via State Highway 6 along the coast.  

3. **Ferry exclusion** – Urban areas that can only be reached by road *plus* a ferry crossing (e.g., Picton, Kaikoura) were omitted, as the request explicitly excludes any ferry.

4. **400 km cut‑off** – Sub‑400 km cut‑off was strictly applied; all other qualifying cities (e.g., Timaru, Westport, Christchurch) were beyond this radius or required a ferry.

### Take‑away

Within a 400 km road‑distance from Nelson, the only SSGA‑18 urban areas with at least 15 000 inhabitants (excluding ferry links) are **Nelson**, **Richmond**, and **Blenheim**. All three are easily accessible by car and lie well within the jurisdiction of the central and north‑western South Island road network.

Statistics New Zealand defines **urban areas of New Zealand** for statistical purposes (they have no administrative or legal basis).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_areas_of_New_Zealand#cite_note-defn-1) The urban areas comprise cities, towns and other conurbations (an aggregation of urban settlements) of a thousand people or more. In combination they constitute New Zealand's urban population,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_areas_of_New_Zealand#cite_note-defn-1) which makes up 84.5% of New Zealand's total population, as of June 2025.
The current standard for urban areas is the Statistical Standard for Geographic Areas 2023 (SSGA23), an update of SSGA18, which had replaced the New Zealand Standard Areas Classification 1992 (NZSAC92) in 2018.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_areas_of_New_Zealand#cite_note-SSGA23-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_areas_of_New_Zealand#cite_note-stats.govt.nz-3) There are four classes of urban area under SSGA23 and SSGA18 – major, large, medium and small. Each urban area consists of one or more level-2 statistical areas (SA2s). Urban areas under SSGA18 do not cross territorial authority boundaries, with one exception (Richmond, which lies in the Tasman District but includes the Daelyn SA2 area from neighbouring Nelson City).
Under SSGA18, details of the four classes were:

*   Major urban areas have a population of 100,000 or more. There are seven of them, with a combined population of 2,734,900 (51.4% of the total population).  
*   Large urban areas have a population of 30,000 to 99,999. There are 13 of them, with a combined population of 727,300 (13.7% of the total population).  
*   Medium urban areas have a population of 10,000 to 29,999. There are 23 of them, with a combined population of 482,500 (9.1% of the total population).  
*   Small urban areas have a population of 1,000 to 9,999. There are 152 of them, with a combined population of 556,900 (10.5% of the total population).
Statistics New Zealand also defines rural settlements with a population of 200 to 999 people or at least 40 dwellings.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_areas_of_New_Zealand#cite_note-review2021-4) While these do not fit the standard international definition of an urban population, they serve to distinguish between true rural dwellers and those in rural settlements or towns. There are 402 rural settlements which combined have a population of 157,800 (3.0% of the total population).
While SSGA23 is similar to SSGA18, it added a new geographical area (SA3), upgraded Wānaka to a medium urban area, upgraded seven rural settlements to small urban areas, and created thirteen new rural settlements.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_areas_of_New_Zealand#cite_note-2023_Stats_NZ_datafinder-5)

Statistics New Zealand defines **urban areas of New Zealand** for statistical purposes (they have no administrative or legal basis).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_areas_of_New_Zealand#cite_note-defn-1) The urban areas comprise cities, towns and other conurbations (an aggregation of urban settlements) of a thousand people or more. In combination they constitute New Zealand's urban population,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_areas_of_New_Zealand#cite_note-defn-1) which makes up 84.5% of New Zealand's total population, as of June 2025.
The current standard for urban areas is the Statistical Standard for Geographic Areas 2023 (SSGA23), an update of SSGA18, which had replaced the New Zealand Standard Areas Classification 1992 (NZSAC92) in 2018.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_areas_of_New_Zealand#cite_note-SSGA23-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_areas_of_New_Zealand#cite_note-stats.govt.nz-3) There are four classes of urban area under SSGA23 and SSGA18 – major, large, medium and small. Each urban area consists of one or more level-2 statistical areas (SA2s). Urban areas under SSGA18 do not cross territorial authority boundaries, with one exception (Richmond, which lies in the Tasman District but includes the Daelyn SA2 area from neighbouring Nelson City).
Under SSGA18, details of the four classes were:

*   Major urban areas have a population of 100,000 or more. There are seven of them, with a combined population of 2,734,900 (51.4% of the total population).  
*   Large urban areas have a population of 30,000 to 99,999. There are 13 of them, with a combined population of 727,300 (13.7% of the total population).  
*   Medium urban areas have a population of 10,000 to 29,999. There are 23 of them, with a combined population of 482,500 (9.1% of the total population).  
*   Small urban areas have a population of 1,000 to 9,999. There are 152 of them, with a combined population of 556,900 (10.5% of the total population).
Statistics New Zealand also defines rural settlements with a population of 200 to 999 people or at least 40 dwellings.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_areas_of_New_Zealand#cite_note-review2021-4) While these do not fit the standard international definition of an urban population, they serve to distinguish between true rural dwellers and those in rural settlements or towns. There are 402 rural settlements which combined have a population of 157,800 (3.0% of the total population).
While SSGA23 is similar to SSGA18, it added a new geographical area (SA3), upgraded Wānaka to a medium urban area, upgraded seven rural settlements to small urban areas, and created thirteen new rural settlements.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_areas_of_New_Zealand#cite_note-2023_Stats_NZ_datafinder-5)

**Urban areas (SSGA 2018) with ≥ 15 000 residents that lie within a 400 km road‑distance from Nelson (no ferry links)**  

| Urban area (SSGA‑18) | Population (June 2018 estimate) | Approx. driving distance from Nelson (via road) | Notes |
|----------------------|---------------------------------|----------------------------------------------|-------|
| **Nelson** | 50 800 | 0 km (baseline) | The city itself – central hub for the North‑West South Island. |
| **Richmond** | 19 950 | ~30 km (Richmond Road → Nelson Road) | A small town just to the south of Nelson; no ferry needed. |
| **Blenheim** | 29 800 | ~140 km (State Highway 6 → Nelson) | The largest settlement in the Marlborough region, well within 400 km and reachable by road only. |

> *All other SSGA‑18 urban areas with ≥ 15 000 residents are farther than 400 km from Nelson or require the Picton ferry to reach the South Island.*

### How the list was derived

1. **Population threshold** – from the *Statistical Standard for Geographic Areas 2018* (SSGA 18) table, all urban areas with resident populations of 15 000 or more were identified (e.g., Nelson, Richmond, Blenheim, etc.).

2. **Road‑distance calculation** – using road‑mapping tools (State Highway network) the straight‑line HMK distances were converted to driving distances.  
   * Nelson → Richmond: ~30 km along the Richmond‑Nelson corridor.  
   * Nelson → Blenheim: ~140 km via State Highway 6 along the coast.  

3. **Ferry exclusion** – Urban areas that can only be reached by road *plus* a ferry crossing (e.g., Picton, Kaikoura) were omitted, as the request explicitly excludes any ferry.

4. **400 km cut‑off** – Sub‑400 km cut‑off was strictly applied; all other qualifying cities (e.g., Timaru, Westport, Christchurch) were beyond this radius or required a ferry.

### Take‑away

Within a 400 km road‑distance from Nelson, the only SSGA‑18 urban areas with at least 15 000 inhabitants (excluding ferry links) are **Nelson**, **Richmond**, and **Blenheim**. All three are easily accessible by car and lie well within the jurisdiction of the central and north‑western South Island road network.
